stature.source: typical: the drafter's middle for streambank and aspen-edge thickets; tall: FEIS (1-3 m) and Wikipedia (up to 3 m); no record height was read; read 2026-11-10

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a dense, rounded thicket of many straight, prickly, red to grey-brown stems, wider than tall and leafy nearly to the ground; pink single roses in early summer, clusters of red hips from late summer that hang on through winter, the leaves orange-red in fall

description: A deciduous, prickly shrub 0.5-2 m tall whose straight red to grey-brown stems sprout from the root crown and from suckering roots into dense thickets. Its leaves are pinnate, of five to nine sharply toothed leaflets up to 5 cm; fragrant pink five-petalled roses open singly or a few together in early summer, and round red hips about a centimetre across ripen in August and September and hang on the bare stems through the winter. It grows along streambanks, meadow and field edges, in aspen stands, open woods and shrublands across the interior West, from the Yellowstone and Teton valleys to the rims of the Grand Canyon.

season_notes.winter: Bare, prickly red-brown stems hung with red hips above the snow; mule deer and grouse eat the hips.
season_notes.spring: Leaves open in May; elk and deer browse the new growth.
season_notes.summer: Pink roses in June and July, scenting the streambanks; the thickets shelter nesting birds and deer mice.
season_notes.fall: Hips turn red in August and September and the leaves go orange and red before they drop; bears eat the hips.

riparian.water: Grows best where the soil stays moist into summer: streambanks and terraces, the edges of wet meadows and seeps, washes and canyon bottoms, spreading by root suckers; it also stands on drier slopes, field edges and roadsides away from water, more thinly.

range.where: streambanks, meadow edges, aspen stands and sagebrush shrubland of the Yellowstone and Jackson Hole valleys, and the canyons and rims of the Grand Canyon; most of western and central North America from Alaska and Canada to Arizona, New Mexico and Texas

notes: California wild rose (the template) is the library's rose, the same genus and the same suckering thicket habit, flowers and hips; the card makes Woods' rose a little lower (FEIS: 1-3 m, var. woodsii under 1 m; Wikipedia: up to 3 m; height_m 0.5-2 m for the interior West's streambank and aspen-edge stands), with red to grey-brown prickly stems (Wikipedia; FEIS: curved prickles 3-6 mm). Leaves 1.5-13 cm, of 5-9 leaflets to 5 cm (FEIS; Wikipedia: sharp-toothed leaflets up to 5 cm), so leaf_size_m 0.08 for the whole leaf and the template's pinnate_compound shape. Flowers five-petalled, any shade of pink, fragrant, to 2.5 cm (Wikipedia; FEIS: 1.5-2 cm), singly or in few-flowered clusters, May-July (Wikipedia), May-August in Utah (FEIS); June-July for the Yellowstone and Teton tiles is the drafter's reading. Hips red, some over 1 cm (Wikipedia; FEIS: 0.75-1.5 cm, in clusters), ripening August-September (Wikipedia); that they hang on through the winter follows from FEIS (mule deer eat the hips heavily in winter, sharp-tailed grouse eat them in winter), hence months 8 to 2 as the template has them. Spreads by root-crown sprouts, root suckers and layering (FEIS). Habitat: streambanks and riparian areas, dry slopes, open woods, hillsides, washes, roadsides, canyons and rocky ravines, an understory of Rocky Mountain Douglas-fir and quaking aspen stands, codominant on some riparian sites (FEIS); open woods, plains, stream banks, stony slopes and disturbed areas (Wikipedia). Moderately shade tolerant but more vigorous and fruitful in full sun, top-killed by fire and sprouting back from the root crown, a coloniser of burns, old fields, roadsides and eroded ground (FEIS), hence shade 0.4 and disturbed 1.3. The riparian zones and permanence are the drafter's judgement from those habitats (it grows on streambanks and also on dry slopes, so permanence any). Elevation: Wyoming 1370-3500 m, Utah 850-3350 m, Colorado 1070-2740 m, Arizona 430-2440 m (FEIS, given in feet). The Yellowstone, Grand Teton and Grand Canyon placing is from the brief. Eaters: FEIS names mule deer, elk, white-tailed deer and moose (important browse, spring and summer foliage; mule deer eat the hips heavily in winter), grizzly bears (the plant, and hips in Idaho and Montana), sharp-tailed grouse (hips in winter) and porcupines; upland birds, nongame birds and waterfowl nest in it and deer mice, voles, prairie dogs and pocket gophers use it for cover. The black bear stands in for the grizzly, the mallard for nesting waterfowl and the American robin for the nesting songbirds; moose, white-tailed deer, sharp-tailed grouse, porcupine, voles of the Rockies, prairie dogs and pocket gophers are not in the library. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, leaf-on months, the flower and hip density and drawn sizes, and shades_water are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
